Our very civilization is based on copying information, and has been since we were telling each other rocks are not edible. A time-limited, artificial restriction is legally put upon it in order to produce a greater incentive to produce intellectual works. Currently our representatives, bought and paid for, have taken the time-limited provision in the Constitution and changed it from 10 or 15 years or so to essentially "in the fullness of God's plan," seeing as how anyone who sees anything here will be long dust by the time anything is released into the public domain. This is rather obviously a blatant mockery of what it was intended to be, where the public domain would eventually acquire these works, and likely within the lifetime of most people interested in the particular work so they could modify it.

And the public domain! How much of our world is aided by the public domain? Plenty. Look at our popular mythos. We see Cthulhu popping up everywhere, as well as elves and gnomes and an endless array of swords-stuck-in-stones. What isn't there? Pikachus, Italian plumbers and ships named Enterprise, for starters - particularly sci-fi, which wasn't around in much force when the copyright term started growing insanely. The former group was in the public domain; the latter isn't. This leads to continued stagnation of many works, and stifles society in general as well. Plus, it ensures that a lot of works will be forgotten and subsequently lost simply because no one can legally copy them.

Never you mind that some of these markets were CREATED by piracy. PCs had emulation long before retrogaming. Anime and manga got its start with fansubs and scanlations. Companies still get an idea of what to localize by what gets pirated. Microsoft itself has admitted their dominance was helped greatly by piracy. Plus, most works make most of their money in their first few years of being available, and as such said works are left to rot and be lost once their primary marketing period has passed. That's NOT a good thing, even if in theory someone might dust it off and sell it again in 40 years. Not a lot of things are that lucky. Some have even deliberately put their own works out as pirated copies in order to make sure if there's something circulating out there, at least it's good quality, so that people are more likely to buy it. In fact, a lot of pirates buy a lot more media on average.

Patent law, screwed up as it is, is actually a good reference for some of this, to show that the time limit DOES WORK. In fact, the time limit in patent law is about the only thing that works. For a limited time (NOTE - limited!) inventors get the benefit of their patent, and in exchange, at the end of that period - which, unlike copyrights, is a few years, and not long after the creator and everyone who ever cared about the work are dead, on the highly unlikely assumption that copyright laws won't be pushed back repeatedly ad nauseum. Even trademark law is somewhat better, in that you have to "use it or lose it."

Furthermore, the "soft" nature of intellectual property is a great advantage. With things like DRM, the companies are attempting to encumber the IP with the same difficulties with moving and sharing it as a physical good. As such they are trying to force it into having the legal properties of being both IP and a physical good, essentially cheating their part of the deal for their legal protection. Not to mention the fact that they're trying to use licensing agreements as a kudgel to try to dictate what can and cannot be done with their product, e.g. modifying a car with software. Long term, copyright is likely going to be used as a kudgel in an attempt at social control, which is a VERY bad thing. It's made worse by the fact that this will do very little to stop powerful companies who can enforce their will through their deep pockets, and probably continue piracy practices on their own while trying to send the little guy to spend his days breaking rocks into smaller rocks as long as they can to make an example of him.

All this aside - people still need actual media to be made. No question about it. So even if it's free, it isn't necessarily going to come out of nowhere. People are paid to MAKE it, because it is needed. And if they aren't paid, many will do it anyway. While a Kickstarter-esque model would be difficult to work with for entertainment, it likely could be made to work - they're making Star Trek episodes on YouTube, and computers are making that all the more practical all the time. Furthermore, support for many types of IP is important, and providing support is a good way to make a living in and of itself. While I am not entirely against commercial software, FOSS works can and do have business models that will work. If you doubt that, read up on Red Hat Software.

Plus people will do it for free with tools to do so! For all the whining of the commercial Internet about advertising sales, the Internet was based off of a gift economy from the start, at least once the civilian element came about in the 90s. Commercial interests came to the Internet and attempted to harness it for their revenue generation. People can and do produce free content all the time and share it. Computers are making it possible to efficiently make increasingly impressive and capable content all the time with fewer resources. The Internet got along quite fine without trying to shove malware-laced ads down your throat at every turn, followed by whatever pop culture story comes with it, and without attempting to turn the Internet into a giant trap on behalf of Microsoft and Disney. It did so before, and it can do so again, even if all those corporations leeching off the Internet spontaneously combust.

Truth be told, plenty of these laws are more inclined towards protecting COMPANIES, not artists. The artists tend not to end up being ridiculously wealthy anymore. What's going on is that the corporations are attempting to establish choke points over distribution, much as they had before the Internet, and fortify their defenses there, acting as extremely expensive, aggressive brokers between producers and consumers, despite the increasing obsolescence of the business model. These impositions are being bought and paid for by companies who find it cheaper to simply kill competition in the womb than try to innovate or adapt. They feel the world owes them a profit. It most certainly does not, especially from companies like movie studios that cook the books to duck taxes. Many innovations that we now depend on were made primarily due to the free exchange of ideas and material. If you tried to encumber the Internet with trying to make everything "licensed" you wouldn't have an Internet, right now we wouldn't be having this conversation because we would at best be on an extra-fancy Compuserve or AOL that was too slow and too expensive to use for anything even close to similar to Voat.

Believe it or not, I would favor stronger copyright if it were an actual reasonable, SHORT time limit Now there is no limit in practice, corporations are trying to seize works in the public domain (and to have some extent succeeded), and leeching off of the general public for the enrichment of a relatively small number of people at the expense of society at large in innumerable ways. Additionally the provisions in SOPA and laws like it stifle free speech directly and set extremely dangerous precedents. I would also be in favor of stronger copyright laws WITHOUT absurdities such as tons of surveillance, equating every download as a lost sale, and making private copying worthy of a felony record and prison time, despite the fact that, for a historic example, VCR did not destroy television despite insistence it would. But the companies are not going for something more reasonable - they want you scared into submission and dependent on their products, which will, they hope, legally bind you to their dictates in an ever-increasing manner.

With all these things in mind, I would rather fix copyright, but if I had to pick 'stronger SOPA-backed copyright' and 'no copyright' right now, 'stronger SOPA-backed copyright' would have a bullet through its skull in the time it took me to type this sentence, with no regrets at all. It would be unfortunate, but ultimately it would benefit everyone who didn't own shares in a media conglomerate greatly. SOPA must be destroyed and no laws of similar composition passed. Ever.
